title: Lineage-Specific Mechanisms of Cell Cycle Timing Control
text:
Proper control over the cell cycle is essential to development, homeostasis, and regeneration. The regulation
of differentiation and the specification of cell fates has been extensively studied, as have the fundamental
mechanisms of cell cycle control, but ubiquitous correlations observed between cell fate and the cell cycle
have not been studied in detail. To understand how cell fate regulates the duration of the cell cycle and how
changes in the duration of the cell cycle influence cell fate, we will employ a combination of cell lineage tracing,
spatial transcriptomics, and an evolutionary approach to studying the structure of developmental lineages.

title: Deciphering the Genetic Architecture of Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction
text:
The genetic architecture of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is poorly understood, limiting
drug discovery in this morbid, prevalent and difficult-to-treat condition. To date, genomic discovery has been
limited by poor phenotyping, lack of echocardiograms in genetic biobanks and parsimonious use of biological
data to define HFpEF. To overcome this limitation, this proposal aims to decipher the genomic basis of HFpEF
and identify causal gene-protein pathways driving its pathogenesis.

title: Leveraging epidemiological data to inform the development of a just-in-time adaptive intervention for young adults co-using e-cigarettes and cannabis
text: Emerging evidence indicates that young adults from Hawaii use e-cigarettes and cannabis at higher rates than others but past research has not examined co-use. The current phased study will utilize epidemiological data from two sources to guide the development of a Just-in-Time Adaptive Intervention (JITAI) for young adults ages 18-30 from Hawaii who are the most susceptible to co-use of e-cigarettes and cannabis. Following pilot work, a randomized controlled trial of the JITAI will examine the impact of the new intervention on frequency of e-cigarette, cannabis, and co-use and related problems.

title: Dissecting von Willebrand factor secretory machinery for therapeutic vulnerabilities
text:
von Willebrand factor (vWF) is a plasma protein required for normal blood coagulation. von Willebrand disease,
caused by deficiency of vWF, is the most common bleeding disorder in humans, but high vWF levels in the
blood also increases risk of cardiovascular morbidity. We propose to study how vWF secretion from its
vascular stores is controlled by directly characterizing the proteins required for its regulated secretion, with the
ultimate goal of identifying novel therapeutic targets for treatment of diseases associated with vWF deficiency
or excess.

title: Neural mechanisms regulating glucose homeostasis
text: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2D) is the major form of human diabetes, accounting for approximately 90–95% of diagnosed diabetes cases in the United States. Our research is designed to provide insight into how the brain contributes to blood glucose regulation in T2D. Specifically, we aim to identify the neural factors responsible for the development of T2D and address a novel liver glucose metabolism-based mechanism of this disease.

title: Mechanistic characterization and rational design of Lassa virus entry inhibitors
text:
Small-molecule drugs offer distinct advantages as Lassa virus (LASV) therapeutics: they can be target-specific,
cost-effective, scalable, fast-acting, orally bioavailable, and accessible in resource-limited regions. Here we will
advance LASV-specific lead compounds identified through two large-scale high-throughput screens by
elucidating their mechanisms of action and optimizing their potency and pharmacokinetic properties. These
studies will guide the development of effective small-molecule inhibitors of a major emerging pathogen.

title: Photoaffinity and Multi-Omic Analysis of Targets Pathways Driving Synthetic Opioid-Induced Toxicity and Reversal
text:
Ultra-Potent Synthetic opioids such as fentanyl, carfentanil, and nitazenes can cause severe toxicity that is not
always fully reversed by current opioid antidotes. This project will define naloxone-insensitive mechanisms of
fentanyl toxicity, build a mechanistic map of actionable pathways, and use translational prioritization to identify
and test candidate post-exposure reversal agents. The work is expected to provide new targets and
reversal/mitigation strategies that can inform development of next-generation medical countermeasures for
structurally diverse UPS opioids.

title: Pilot Research
text: The Pilot Research Project Core actively seeks, assesses, and supports novel and forward-thinking feasibility (pilot) studies within the UIUC Neuroproteomics and Neurometabolomics Center on Cell-Cell Signaling. Our Core and Center thrive when we facilitate the achievements of promising young investigators who are new to our 'omics measurement capabilities or addiction research, while also encouraging experienced researchers to extend their research to substance use/misuse and addiction. The selected pilot projects will have access to our considerable Center resources available through our scientific cores—Sampling and Separation, Molecular Profiling and Characterization, and Bioinformatics, Data Analytics and Predictive Modeling—to generate the data required for continued research and potential for longer-term support. The Pilot Research Project Core ensures that the NIDA / neuroscience research community continues to take advantage of the opportunities and expertise offered by our Center. Applicants who propose feasibility studies, who want to explore how to incorporate ‘omics data into their research, or what to start a new direction that fits the NIDA and Center research areas may qualify for support from the Pilot Core. To improve overall Center capabilities that will benefit multiple users, the Pilot Core will also support small technical, methodological, or conceptual developments from staff and users to improve Center measurement and informatics capabilities. Toward those goals, we outline three exemplary initial pilot projects targeting neuropeptides, transmitters, and proteins that are involved in multiple aspects of drug use. The first project aims to identify substrates of a receptor linked to addiction and neural plasticity. The second project focuses on characterizing neuropeptides to understand genetic factors contributing to oxycodone-related phenotypes and their role in opioid use disorder development. The third project aims to perform single-cell transcriptomics measurements for the project investigator, with the developed technology also benefiting other Center projects. We will solicit new proposals each year, and support up to eight additional projects for competitive review by the Core over the next five years. The Core has a rigorous process in place to solicit, assess, and select Pilot projects. Overall, the Pilot Research Project Core, an important component of the Center for Neuroproteomics and Neurometabolomics on Cell-Cell Signaling, encourages the use of cutting-edge technology, fosters cross-disciplinary collaboration, and accelerates progress in addiction research.

title: Light Microscopy Digital Imaging
text: Abstract Light Microcopy & Digital Imaging (LMDI-SR) Light microscopy and digital imaging is integral to COHCCC’s research mission. The LMDI-SR provides a wide range of instruments that allow investigators to image numerous sample types in a variety of carriers such as slides, well plates, culture dishes, and live animals. Specific Aims for LMDI-SR: Aim 1. Provide support for COHCCC Members requiring expertise in light microscopy and digital image protocols. Aim 2. Acquisition of imaging data for principal investigators. Aim 3. Provide sophisticated image analysis and image presentation techniques to investigators. The LMDI-SR has 8 widefield microscope systems that have imaging capabilities in brightfield, fluorescence, differential interference contrast, phase contrast, and structured illumination (Apotome). The LMDI-SR has 5 systems that provide live-cell imaging services that include precise temperature control and CO2 delivery and a system that allows imaging under hypoxic conditions. The Zeiss confocal microscope systems (LSM700, LSM880, LSM900) are the most advanced available and are equipped with Airyscan super-resolution detectors that can increase the resolution and signal to noise ratio two-fold over confocal imaging. The LMDI-SR has two systems capable of 2-photon intra-vital imaging in live mice and rats. The Leica LMD7000 enables researchers to collect laser microdissected samples from slide mounted tissues, as well as live cells, which in turn can then be further analyzed via next generation sequencing, PCR, or mass spectrometry. The LMDI-SR has added the Fluidigm Hyperion imaging mass cytometer to its services providing sophisticated multiparameter imaging data by ablating metal tagged antibodies from tissue samples. The LMDI-SR is directed by Dr Brian Armstrong who has extensive experience in light microscopic imaging and analysis and is supported by a highly trained staff (2 FTEs). The user base has access to the shared resource through iLab. In addition to extensive project-specific practical imaging training users also receive instruction in safety and the ethical collection of scientific imaging data. The LMDI-SR provides several professional software programs such as Image Pro Premier, AMIRA, Imaris, Autoquant, and Visiopharm that can be used to analyze and quantify imaging data, and the staff are well versed in the proper methods for handling large and complicated imaging data sets. title: Unlocking the Potential of the GSC-Associated lncRNA GIHCG as a Therapeutic Target in Glioblastoma
text:
This study aims to determine the role of the long non-coding RNA, GIHCG, associated with
glioblastoma stem cells, in promoting the initiation and progression of glioblastoma. The findings
are expected to offer valuable insights that could lead to new treatment strategies for this
aggressive form of brain cancer.

title: Genomic determinants and ecological interactions of human associated Akkermansia grown on core human milk oligosaccharides
text:
The current paradigm that Akkermansia are beneficial bacteria of the human gut microbiota is based on an
incomplete understanding of their basic biology and ecology. This project will define the metabolic strategies
and ecological dynamics of diverse species of human associated Akkermansia with the long-term goal of
developing targeted, therapeutic uses of Akkermansia, either through stimulating endogenous strains or by
administering specific strains during critical life-stages or under specific disease states. This work is significant
as it will help lead to the rational design of effective therapies involving diverse Akkermansia in a context
dependent manner.

title: Thrombospondin 4 regulates adaptive ER stress responseRenewal - Resubmission - 1
text:
The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response appears is a universal feature of all cardiomyopathies as
well as healing after cardiac injury or disease initiation. Here we have identified a novel function for
thrombospondin3 (Thbs3) and Thbs4 as intracellular regulators of the ER pathway shuttling of membrane
attachment complexes, such as the integrins and dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC), which impacts the
stability of the plasma membrane in heart and skeletal muscle. Understanding the mechanisms whereby the
Thbs proteins regulate cellular attachment complexes in the plasma membrane has profound medical
relevance as many forms of heart disease are associated with altered membrane strength and cellular
connection to the extracellular matrix.

title: Mentoring and Research in Cardiovascular Device Evaluation
text: This grant will support protected time for Dr. Robert Yeh to provide mentorship for junior investigators interested in patient-oriented cardiovascular research, with the scientific goal to evaluate how the large amounts of data collected each day in the routine course of clinical care can best be employed to study commonly used devices to treat serious heart conditions. The study will use state-of-the-science approaches for data analysis to examine whether several high-risk cardiovascular devices are being used safely and effectively in the United States today. The results of this research will determine how ubiquitous data collected by registries, health systems and payers, and advanced causal inference methods, can best be combined to improve our present and future understanding of new medical devices.

title: Computational tools and quantitative analyses of genome structure evolution
text:
Chromosomal variation plays an important role in several biological processes and is associated with multiple
traits, yet the forces driving and maintaining this variation are not fully understood. This proposal tackles
challenges regarding the evolution of two major features of the genomic landscape: chromosome inversions
and sex chromosomes. By developing computational tools necessary for genomic analysis and by testing core
hypotheses of the evolution of large genomic features, this work will make important strides in our
understanding of how and why the structure of the genome changes through evolutionary time.

title: Modeling IDH Mutant Gliomas by Genetic Engineering of Brain Organoid
text:
Glioma is the second cause of cancer death in young adult under 40 years old. The proposed research
will develop a model which could be used to study how these tumors are formed. The studies will
provide understanding of how genetic mutations contribute to tumor formation and thus lead to novel
therapy. The research is relevant to the VA where numerous cases of brain tumors were diagnosed and
treated.

title: Developing Computational Tools for Predicting and Designing Function-Enhancing Enzyme Variants
text:
Natural enzymes present exquisite control of efficiency and selectivity of chemical reactions, but how to
predict enzyme variants to transform non-native chemical processes is broadly recognized as a “Holy Grail” in
chemistry and biology because it will allow researchers to find effective enzyme variants to degrade
environmental pollutants, conduct late-stage functionalization of drug molecules, and treat food allergies.
Directed evolution has been widely applied to identify optimal enzyme variants for non-native reactions, but how
to accelerate the screening cycles remains a critical roadblock due to the unknown relationship between
sequence, structure, and kinetics for enzyme catalysis. My research program emphasizes developing
computational platforms for the identification of function-enhancing enzyme variants to transform non-native
enzymatic reactions, with an ultimate goal of delivering enabling computational tools for virtual prediction and
design of function-enhancing enzyme variants for biomedical and biocatalytic uses.

title: Translational Genomics Core
text: The Translational Genomics Core (TGC) of the Louisiana Cancer Research Consortium (LCRC) was initially created as a genomics/sequencing facility to support basic research infrastructure needs within the School of Medicine. Support of Phase I and II of COBRE “Mentoring Translational Research in Louisiana” and from the LSU School of Medicine and the Louisiana Cancer Research Center (LCRC) has facilitated TGC development into a state-of-the-art institutional facility capable of implementing a variety of next generation sequencing (NGS) protocols including whole transcriptome, RNASeq, whole exome sequencing, and array-based methylation and SNP analysis, single-cell sequencing and chromatin-immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq). The TGC has served multiple projects through the establishment of service contracts and collaborations at the institutional, local and national levels. The TGC is ideally positioned to support the Phase 2 COBRE “Center for Translational Viral Oncology” (CTVO) application. As in the first phase of the CTVO, the Research Project Leaders (RPLs) will have a discounted pricing structure, comprehensive training, instrumentation access, troubleshooting advice, and data analysis assistance that is linked to multi-institutional informatics pipelines, including the CTVO BBC. The TGC has been instrumental in the acquisition of two P20-SPORE grants: 1) P20CA202922 (PIs Miele and Meade), and a collaboration with Moffitt Cancer Center in Tampa, FL, in which the TGC Director is a research project PI; 2) 5P20CA233374 (PIs Ochoa, Miele). The TGC is constantly evolving and updating instrumentation and protocols to ensure that RPLs in Phase 2 CVTO will have cutting-edge capacity to generate high quality data. Latest acquisitions are 10X genomics single-cell and tissue localized sequencing. Dr. Zabaleta maintains a constant collaboration with Dr. Chindo Hicks, Director of the Bioinformatics and Genomics Program in the Department of Genetics, School of Medicine, LSUHSC-New Orleans and CTVO BBC Co-director as well as pipelines to Tulane University Cancer and Viral Bioinformatics through Dr. Melody Badoo. Drs Zabaleta and Hicks coordinate the sequencing (Dr. Zabaleta) and bioinformatics (Dr. Hicks) to provide the best information to the requesting investigator. Research capacity developments strengthen the propensity for Phase 2 CTVO research project and pilot study success and likelihood for NIH funding.

title: Modeling dynamic CD8+ T cell-virus interactions in post-treatment control of HIV
text:
There is no cure for HIV. In this Project, we will use a novel and powerful reagent that we have developed to
deeply characterize the HIV-specific immune response as it responds to viral reactivation after antiretroviral
therapy is stopped in order to identify characteristics that drive control of the infection in this setting. This
knowledge can then be used to directly improve the design of T cell-based therapies for HIV cure.

title: The role of VacA in Helicobacter pylori-host cell cholesterol homeostasis
text:
Infection with Helicobacter pylori, a bacterium that colonizes the stomachs of half the world’s population, is the
primary risk factor for the development of peptic ulcers and gastric cancer. This proposal will examine how H.
pylori uses its secreted toxin, VacA, to manipulate host cell cholesterol metabolism in order to acquire an
essential nutrient. By uncovering mechanisms of VacA-induced cholesterol dysregulation, this research will
provide fundamental insights into the pathogenesis of H. pylori infection and H. pylori-mediated gastric diseases.

title: Mechanisms of sperm chromatin remodeling in vivo and in vitro
text:
Infertility affects one in six couples worldwide, with men and women equally likely to have fertility problems. In
men, known genetic factors account for ~10-15% of total infertility cases, whereas the remaining ~35-40%
cases have an unknown etiology. Therefore, a comprehensive understanding of the genetic and molecular
programs involved in proper germ cell development is required for development of better diagnostics and
effective therapies.
